summary: This experimental document describes ways to anonymize IP flow data and export anonymized data with IPFIX. It categorizes common schemes, defines parameters for describing them, and gives guidance on export and storage. An information model supports describing which fields were anonymized and how.

plainLanguage.summary: Network records show who talked to whom. This explains how to hide identities, like blacking out names, and how to say how the hiding was done.

subtitle: Techniques and metadata for hiding identities in network flow records.

tldr.problem: Network flow data is valuable for analysis but reveals who communicated with whom and when, creating privacy risks when shared across organizational boundaries or with research communities.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC categorizes anonymization techniques (truncation, permutation, binning, noise addition) and defines metadata fields to describe how anonymization was applied to flow fields, enabling consistent anonymized export via IPFIX.
tldr.outcome: Organizations can publish anonymized network flow data while documenting the techniques used, allowing researchers and analysts to understand the protection level and utility of shared datasets.

today: RFC 6235 remains the primary specification for anonymization export in IPFIX. It is Experimental, reflecting ongoing research into anonymization attacks and defenses. The techniques and metadata model are deployed in network measurement infrastructures where researchers require both utility and privacy protection.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The IP Flow Information Export (IPFIX) protocol standardizes how network flow data is collected and shared, removing technical barriers to publishing flow data across organizations, with research communities, and for network security analysis. However, wider sharing creates privacy risks: IP flow data can identify individual users and the networks they use. This RFC provides techniques and metadata to anonymize flow data before sharing, protecting privacy while retaining the data's analytical value.

The document emphasizes that anonymization decisions depend on the specific data source, purpose, and deanonymization risk involved. Exporters must choose appropriate techniques and acknowledge that anonymization alone is not a complete privacy solution; other protections like encryption are also important.
sections.plainLanguage: Network traffic data can reveal private information. This explains how to hide the information while keeping the data useful, and how to say which hiding method was used.

sections.title: Anonymization Techniques
sections.content:
The RFC categorizes anonymization into two dimensions: recoverability (whether the real data can be recovered from the anonymized data) and countability (whether the number of unique values is preserved). This produces four classes:

  • Generalization: maps multiple real values to one anonymized value, losing information.
  • Direct substitution: each real value maps to exactly one anonymized value, preserving counts.
  • Set substitution: allows one real value to map to multiple anonymized values.
  • One-way substitution: non-recoverable without additional knowledge.

For IP addresses, the RFC describes truncation (zero out low-order bits), reverse truncation (zero out high-order bits), permutation (replace with a random address), and prefix-preserving pseudonymization (preserve network structure while anonymizing). Similar techniques apply to MAC addresses, timestamps, and counters, each with different trade-offs between privacy protection and data utility.
sections.plainLanguage: Different hiding methods preserve different information. Some blur everything equally; others keep the network structure visible so you can still see which networks talked to each other. Some methods can be reversed if you know the secret; others cannot.

sections.title: Describing Anonymization
sections.content: Anonymized data is only useful if receivers understand how it was transformed. The RFC defines parameters to describe each technique: stability (whether the same input always produces the same output), truncation length (how many bits were removed), bin map (for binning, which values go into which bin), permutation function parameters (for permutation, the secret key), and shift amount (for time shifts). However, some parameters (the permutation key, shift amount, bin mapping) SHOULD NOT be exported, as they could be used to reverse the anonymization.
sections.plainLanguage: You need to say how the data was hidden. Did you hide the same thing the same way every time, or change it each time? Did you keep some parts visible?

sections.title: IPFIX Export and Metadata
sections.content:
IPFIX can export anonymized data and bind anonymization metadata to it using Anonymization Records and an Anonymization Options Template. Each anonymization record describes which field in which template was anonymized and what technique was applied. Three key information elements are defined:

  • anonymizationTechnique: identifies the technique (undefined, none, precision degradation, binning, enumeration, permutation, structured permutation, reverse truncation, noise, or offset).
  • anonymizationFlags: bit flags describing stability class and special modifications (perimeter-based policies, low-order bits unchanged).
  • informationElementIndex: disambiguates when a template contains multiple instances of the same field.

Anonymization records SHOULD be exported after the templates they describe and MUST be scoped to the templates within the transport session in which they are sent.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send the hidden data, you also send labels saying 'this field was blurred with method X' and 'this part stays the same every time' or 'this part changes each time'. This helps people understand what they can and cannot do with the data.

sections.title: Deployment and Guidelines
sections.content:
Anonymization can be applied at three points in the IPFIX architecture: at the exporting process itself, at a mediator between metering and collection, or at a collecting process before storage in IPFIX files. The RFC provides practical guidelines to avoid leaking anonymized information through side channels:

  • Choose information elements whose data type matches the anonymization technique.
  • Anonymize the IPFIX message header's export time to match anonymized timestamp data, preventing relationships from being exploited.
  • Avoid using IPv4 interface addresses as the Observation Domain ID if addresses are structure-preserving-anonymized, as this can break the anonymization.
  • Anonymize or omit exporting process addresses in options templates that might relate to internal network structure.
  • Filter or exclude special-use address space (RFC 5735, RFC 5156) to prevent pattern recognition attacks.

The RFC notes that no anonymization is perfect; all techniques are subject to ongoing research on attacks and defenses.
sections.plainLanguage: When you hide the main data, be careful not to accidentally reveal the secret through other information you send along with it, like the time you sent the message or the address of your router.
